facts.title: Priority 1 Air Rescue Operations (Arizona), LP
facts.agency: Department of Homeland Security, United States Coast Guard
facts.procurement_type: negotiated procurement (RFP under RFO parts 12 and 15), small business set-aside
facts.background: The Coast Guard issued RFP No. 70Z02326R93150001 on June 18, 2026, under the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul parts 12 and 15, and amended it seven times. The small business set-aside seeks design, fabrication, delivery, installation, and support of three advanced training devices. The devices are an MH-60T level 7 flight training device, a mixed-reality hoist training simulator, and a deployable hoist training simulator. All three must be interoperable and able to operate in a linked, real-time, synchronized mode with latency not exceeding 50 milliseconds. The agency historically relied on classroom instruction, part-task trainers, and operational flight time to train aircrews. The Aviation Training Center reviewed flight mechanic training then provided under a contract with the protester and concluded that agency-owned hoist simulators would be beneficial. A working group recommended acquiring at least three H-60 simulators and a hoist trainer, and market research indicated that a prime contractor integrating subcontracted specialty vendors was the industry standard. The Secretary of Homeland Security approved the Commandant's contract approval memorandum on March 12, 2026. On August 3, 2026, before proposals were due, the protester filed this protest challenging the combination of the requirements.

protester_grounds.claim: The RFP unduly restricts competition by unnecessarily combining the requirements for three simulator types into one solicitation, in violation of CICA's full and open competition and restrictive provisions requirements.
The RFP's hoist training simulator specifications require equipment specific to one manufacturer, showing bias in favor of that manufacturer.

facts.agency_position: The agency contends that combining the three devices under one solicitation is reasonable given its redesign of flight crew training and is critical to safety and effectiveness. It argues that interoperability is the reason for a single solicitation and that a single contractor must integrate the components to achieve reliable training. It submitted a declaration from the Aviation Training Center commanding officer supporting this position. For the manufacturer-specific claim, the agency stated it would amend the RFP to use generic terms, and it later did so during the protest.
facts.record_facts_protected: The RFP requires the three devices to operate in a linked, synchronized mode with latency not exceeding 50 milliseconds. The Commandant's memorandum projected that training flights per mechanic would fall from 11 to 6 and that annual flight hour savings would exceed $15 million. Market research described a prime contractor leading production and integration, with subcontracted specialty vendors, as the industry standard. The commanding officer's declaration states that separately procured simulators could use incompatible models and exceed the latency limit. The agency cites two prior instances in which split simulator procurements led to interoperability failures.
